chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man came to Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) with another man, and said, 'This one has slandered me,' and there was no proof for him. So he said, 'O Amir al-Mu'minin! Make me swear an oath.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no swearing of an oath regarding a Penalty (Hadd), and there is no retaliation regarding a bone.'

key_terms.قَذَفَنِي: He has slandered me (specifically in the context of Hadd al-Riddah or Hadd al-Qadhf)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on taking an oath in Hadd cases and applying Qisas to bones according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) succinctly articulates two foundational jurisprudential maxims: the exclusion of oaths from Hadd penalties and the limitation of Qisas to flesh rather than bones. This narration, recorded in Al-Kafi, highlights the distinct procedural differences between Hadd (fixed punishments) and Qisas (retaliation), emphasizing that while oaths may suffice in civil disputes, they are insufficient for establishing Hadd crimes like slander (Qadhf). The reference to 'bones' underscores the physical limits of retributive justice, distinguishing it from the more rigorous evidentiary standards required for Hadd.
